label: q2-physics
topic: Q2 binding-affinity prediction: the physics that models skip
summary: Binding affinity is hard in principle because the quantity is a small difference of large, compensating terms (dG = dH - TdS; a 10 cal/mol/K entropy change is 2.98 kcal/mol at 298 K), the useful resolution is 0.5-1.4 kcal/mol (5-10x in K; RT ln10 = 1.364 kcal/mol), and the labels are noisy: independent experiments agree to only 0.77-0.95 kcal/mol RMS (Ross 2023), with R2max about 0.81 on public Ki sets (Kramer 2012). Relative FEP reaches median pairwise RMSE 1.08 kcal/mol against an experimental 0.85 on a carefully prepared benchmark, near the floor, but only after protonation, tautomers, poses, waters and flexible loops were fixed by hand. Learned scoring functions reach RMSE 1.3-1.5 pK (1.8-2.1 kcal/mol) and a pure lookup of similar training complexes gets 1.517 pK on the leaky CASF split, so much benchmark skill is memorisation (Graber 2025). A Lean statement can capture the arithmetic and statistical ceilings (log conversion, noise floor, Kd = koff/kon, Cheng-Prusoff, cycle additivity); the sizes of sigma, prevalence of compensation, water and protonation effects, and model generalisation are empirical. No Lean was compiled in this run.
lay_summary: Drug makers want to predict how tightly a small molecule sticks to a protein. The difference between a good and a mediocre drug can be tiny, about the energy of one weak bond, and 1.4 kcal/mol of energy already means a tenfold change in stickiness. It is like weighing a ship's captain by weighing the ship with and without him: two huge numbers, and a small error in either swamps the answer. Even the lab measurements disagree with each other by about that much, so no model can honestly be judged better than the lab noise. Heavy physics simulations get close to that limit but need expert care, while many machine-learning models score well mostly because their test questions resemble their training answers.

findings.claim: A 10-fold change in Kd corresponds to RT ln10 = 1.364 kcal/mol at 298.15 K; 1.4 kcal/mol gives 10.6-fold.
findings.source: own calculation: scripts/q2-physics/arithmetic.py (CODATA R=8.314462 J/mol/K, T=298.15 K, 1 cal=4.184 J)

findings.claim: Lead optimisation needs about 5-fold (roughly 0.95 kcal/mol) resolution in affinity.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1021/ja512751q (abstract via Europe PMC/Crossref); conversion own calc
findings.evidence_quote: the level of accuracy that would be needed to guide lead optimization (∼5× in binding affinity)

findings.claim: Independent experimental measurements of the same protein-ligand pair differ by an RMS of 0.56-0.69 pKi (0.77-0.95 kcal/mol), depending on curation.
findings.source: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-023-01019-9 (PMC10576784 full text), citing Kramer et al.
findings.evidence_quote: the root-mean-square difference between these independent measurements ranged from 0.56 pKi units (0.77 kcal mol−1) to 0.69 pKi units (0.95 kcal mol−1) depending on how the data was curated

findings.claim: Kramer et al. estimate public ChEMBL Ki experimental uncertainty: mean error 0.44 pKi, SD 0.54, median 0.34; maximum squared Pearson R on large datasets 0.81.
findings.evidence_quote: The experimental uncertainty is estimated to yield a mean error of 0.44 pK(i) units, a standard deviation of 0.54 pK(i) units, and a median error of 0.34 pK(i) units. The maximum possible squared Pearson correlation coefficient (R(2)) on large data sets is estimated to be 0.81.

findings.claim: Kramer: models with errors below experimental uncertainty are overtrained, so experimental uncertainty is a natural upper limit on predictive performance (the statement a Lean noise-ceiling theorem would formalise).
findings.evidence_quote: experimental uncertainty defines a natural upper limit to the predictive performance possible. Models that yield errors smaller than the experimental uncertainty are necessarily overtrained.

findings.claim: Ross et al. survey: median RMSE between experimental assays is 0.85 kcal/mol; median pairwise RMSE of FEP+ on their benchmark is 1.08 kcal/mol.
findings.evidence_quote: The median RMSE in the experimental survey is 0.85 kcal mol−1 and the median in the FEP+ benchmark is 1.08 kcal mol−1.

findings.claim: Of 13,732 FEP+ relative binding free energy predictions, 57.5% were within 1 kcal/mol of experiment and 12.9% off by more than 2; among 314,535 experimental pairs 83.0% agreed within 1 kcal/mol and 2.1% differed by more than 2.
findings.evidence_quote: In all 13,732 FEP+ relative binding free energy predictions, 57.5% were within 1 kcal mol−1 of the experimental value and 12.9% differed by more than 2 kcal mol−1

findings.claim: Ross et al.: experimental RMSE is about 1 kcal/mol on average, so FEP matching it on a large diverse set would be an extraordinary challenge; with careful structure preparation FEP can reach accuracy comparable to experimental reproducibility.
findings.evidence_quote: As our experimental reproducibility survey indicated that experimental RMSE is on average ~1 kcal mol−1, it would be an extraordinary challenge to ever have an FEP method that achieves an error truly statistically indistinguishable

findings.claim: FEP accuracy depends on preparation: protonation and tautomeric states of ligand and protein residues are historically difficult to assign; missing loops and flexible regions need care.
findings.evidence_quote: A historically difficult aspect of preparing structures has been the determination of the protonation and tautomeric states of the ligands and the protein binding residues

findings.claim: A trivial memorisation baseline (average labels of the 5 most similar training complexes) reaches Pearson R=0.716, RMSE=1.517 (pK units, about 2.07 kcal/mol) on CASF-2016, competitive with published deep-learning scoring functions: train-test leakage between PDBbind and CASF.
findings.evidence_quote: This algorithm showed competitive CASF2016 prediction root-mean-square error (r.m.s.e.) compared with some published deep-learning-based scoring functions (Pearson R = 0.716, r.m.s.e. = 1.517).

findings.claim: After removing leakage (PDBbind CleanSplit) the search baseline drops to RMSE 1.648, R=0.653; GEMS trained on CleanSplit gets RMSE 1.308, R=0.803 (Pafnucy 1.484/0.746, GenScore 1.362/0.780).
findings.evidence_quote: With a prediction r.m.s.e. of 1.308 and a Pearson correlation of 0.803, GEMS considerably outperforms Pafnucy (r.m.s.e. = 1.484, Pearson R = 0.746) and GenScore (r.m.s.e. = 1.362, Pearson R = 0.780)

findings.claim: The best leakage-free learned scoring function (1.308 pK, 1.78 kcal/mol) is about 1.9-2.3x the experimental pairwise RMS (0.77-0.95 kcal/mol); caveat: different quantities (absolute pK vs relative dG) and different sets.
findings.source: own calculation: arithmetic.py; sources CS and ROSS

findings.claim: On CASF-2016, current scoring functions do better at docking power than at scoring, ranking and screening power.
findings.evidence_quote: the performance of current scoring functions is more promising in terms of docking power than scoring, ranking, and screening power.

findings.claim: Entropy-enthalpy compensation: evidence for severe compensation is weak because errors in measured entropy and enthalpy are large and correlated; a limited form may be common.
findings.evidence_quote: We find the evidence for severe compensation to be weak in light of the large magnitude of and correlation between errors in experimental measurements of entropic and enthalpic contributions to binding, though a limited form of compensation may be common.

findings.claim: Chodera and Mobley recommend assessing changes in binding free energy directly, since entropic and enthalpic changes are hard to predict or measure to useful precision.
findings.evidence_quote: Given the difficulty of predicting or measuring entropic and enthalpic changes to useful precision, or using this information in design, we recommend ligand engineering efforts instead focus on computational and experimental methodologies to directly assess changes in binding free energy.

findings.claim: Illustration: at 298.15 K an entropy change of 10 cal/mol/K is worth T*dS = 2.98 kcal/mol (about 153-fold in K), so dH and TdS terms of several kcal/mol each can cancel to leave dG within the 1.4 kcal/mol scale.
findings.source: own calculation: arithmetic.py (the 153 is exp(2.98/0.5925), computed here)

findings.claim: Water displacement: a ligand change that displaces an ordered water can raise or lower affinity depending on the cost of removing the water versus new interactions; naive ligand-only perturbation can trap the water and mislead.
findings.evidence_quote: the binding affinity may diminish if the free-energy increase due to the removal of the bound water molecule is not more than compensated by the additional interactions of the water-displacing moiety.

findings.claim: Protonation: binding can shift pK and protonation states, making binding pH dependent, though shifts do not occur in every complex and prevalence estimates vary by complex and method.
findings.evidence_quote: While there is no doubt that these changes occur, they do not occur all the time; the estimated prevalence varies, both between individual complexes and by method.

findings.claim: Flexibility: conformational selection may be far more common than believed, and a rise in k_obs with ligand concentration is not unequivocal evidence of induced fit.
findings.evidence_quote: We conclude that conformational selection as a mechanism for a ligand binding to its target may be far more common than currently believed.

findings.claim: Residence time (dissociative half-life of the drug-target complex) is an alternative to Kd/IC50 for optimisation, with potential advantages for duration of effect and selectivity.
findings.evidence_quote: This article presents an alternative perspective on drug optimization in terms of drug-target binary complex residence time, as quantified by the dissociative half-life of the drug-target binary complex.

findings.claim: Kinetics arithmetic: Kd=koff/kon, so Kd=1 nM is reached by (kon 1e6 /M/s, koff 1e-3 /s; residence 1000 s) or (kon 1e8, koff 0.1; residence 10 s): same dG, 100-fold different residence time.
findings.source: own calculation: arithmetic.py (Kd=koff/kon is the definition for 1:1 binding)

findings.claim: Assay conditions: mixing ChEMBL IC50 values from different assays adds moderate noise (SD only 25% larger than for Ki); a Ki-IC50 conversion factor of 2 was most reasonable.
findings.evidence_quote: The standard deviation of IC50 data is only 25% larger than the standard deviation of Ki data, suggesting that mixing IC50 data from different assays, even not knowing assay conditions details, only adds a moderate amount of noise

findings.claim: Cheng-Prusoff (competitive inhibitor): IC50 = Ki(1+[S]/Km). At [S]=Km a 2-fold (0.41 kcal/mol) offset; at [S]=10 Km an 11-fold (1.42 kcal/mol) offset, so assay design alone can exceed the 1.4 kcal/mol scale.
findings.source: own calculation: arithmetic.py; formula is unverified background (standard; the 1973 paper's DOI resolved but no text was read)

findings.claim: Brown et al.: expected model performance is often not supported by the underlying data because of neglected assay and prediction errors.
findings.evidence_quote: the expected performance of many models is simply not supported by the underlying data, because of often neglected effects of assay and prediction errors on the reliability of the predicted outcome.

findings.claim: Merck KGaA prospective FEP+ study: physics-based free energy calculation is regarded as the most rigorous way to estimate binding affinity; large-scale prospective use exposed limitations.
findings.evidence_quote: Physics-based free energy calculations are regarded as the most rigorous way to estimate binding affinity.

findings.claim: Relative FEP is the mature form: it predicts affinity differences for congeneric ligands with enough accuracy to add value in hit-to-lead and lead optimisation.
findings.evidence_quote: RBFE simulations can now predict the affinity differences for congeneric ligands with sufficient accuracy and throughput to deliver considerable value in hit-to-lead and lead optimization efforts.

findings.claim: Noise-ceiling arithmetic: R2max = 1 - sigma^2/Var(obs). Kramer's R2max=0.81 with sigma=0.54 pK corresponds to an observed-label SD of about 1.24 pK (assuming the same sigma).
Cooperativity (binding at one site changing affinity at another) is a distinct non-additive effect; no numeric benchmark was extracted.

key_claims.claim: Experimental replicate disagreement is about 0.8-0.95 kcal/mol RMS (0.56-0.69 pKi), so experimental noise sets a floor on any model's measurable error and a ceiling R2 near 0.81 for large public Ki sets.
key_claims.evidence_quote: the root-mean-square difference between these independent measurements ranged from 0.56 pKi units (0.77 kcal mol−1) to 0.69 pKi units (0.95 kcal mol−1) depending on how the data was curated

key_claims.claim: Rigorous FEP reaches median pairwise RMSE 1.08 kcal/mol vs 0.85 for experiment on a carefully prepared benchmark: near, not at, the noise floor.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The median RMSE in the experimental survey is 0.85 kcal mol−1 and the median in the FEP+ benchmark is 1.08 kcal mol−1.

key_claims.claim: Learned scoring functions are further from the floor (best leakage-free RMSE 1.308 pK, about 1.8 kcal/mol), and a no-physics lookup of similar training complexes gets 1.517 pK on the leaky split, so CASF numbers partly reflect memorisation.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Averaging the affinity label of the five most similar training complexes resulted in an r.m.s.e. of 1.648 and a Pearson correlation of 0.653.

key_claims.claim: 1.4 kcal/mol is a 10.6-fold change in K at 298 K (RT ln10 = 1.364 kcal/mol gives exactly 10-fold).

recommendations: Lean-capturable (theorems from explicit hypotheses): (1) dG = -RT ln K, so a factor 10 in K is RT ln10; (2) noise ceiling: for label = truth + independent noise of variance s^2 with observed variance V, any predictor's squared correlation with the observed label is at most 1 - s^2/V and its expected squared error against one measurement is at least s^2; (3) pairwise replicate RMS = sqrt2 * sigma; (4) additivity of dG around thermodynamic cycles, so an RBFE graph is identifiable only up to a constant; (5) Kd = koff/kon, so equal dG allows different residence times and no function of dG alone predicts residence; (6) Cheng-Prusoff offset; (7) compensation: with dG = dH - T dS, dH and T dS can both move while dG stays fixed, so enthalpy alone does not identify dG; (8) a nearest-neighbour memoriser has error bounded by label variation among similar inputs, so benchmark skill under leakage is not evidence of physics. None of these were compiled in this run; they are proposals.

Empirical (needs data, not Lean): size of sigma per assay type; prevalence and magnitude of compensation; water-network energetics; protonation shifts; induced fit versus selection; cooperativity; whether a given deep model generalises. Test the Lean noise-ceiling statement against public replicate data (ChEMBL pairs, Ross survey) and the CleanSplit versus original PDBbind results.
Convert pK to kcal/mol explicitly (x1.364). Ross reports relative dG pairwise errors, Graber reports absolute pK errors, so do not compare 1.08 kcal/mol and 1.308 pK directly.

No Lean file was written, compiled or checked (repo is read-only here; the lean/ registry contains no affinity statements as far as a grep for noise/reliab/affinity found); recommendations are proposals only.
Kramer's 0.54 pKi SD may refer to pairwise differences; the abstract does not say, so the sqrt2 conversion is applied only to Ross's RMS differences (assumption flagged).

Ross experimental vs FEP+ comparison (0.85 vs 1.08) involves different sets/quantities, so it is suggestive not a strict test; a Gaussian with sigma=1.08 would give 64.6% within 1 kcal/mol versus the reported 57.5% (heavier tails).
